newsitem.title: GERMANY: Strong market lifts German air cargo rates to America.
newsitem.headline: Strong market lifts German air cargo rates to America.

text.p: Air cargo market rates from Germany to the Americas are rising as airlines apply price rises in a strong export market, a Reuters survey showed.
But carriers and forwarders are keenly waiting to see which airlines will drop their cargo fuel surcharges following the recent fall in jet fuel prices, sources said.
Rates to North America have been increased by up to 10 percent by Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, Air Canada, Swissair and others in March.
But the picture is more mixed to Latin America with hikes to Brazil but stable prices for smaller destinations.
Air cargo prices from Germany to South Africa are under strong pressure as passenger flights for the summer holiday season come into service and bring more cargo capacity on to the market.
German forwarders, shippers and other airlines are now waiting to see whether and when Lufthansa Cargo will drop its 10 US cents per kg fuel surcharge after Delta dropped its surcharge on March 13.
Stefan Hass, Delta's regional manager cargo sales and service Europe, claimed Delta had not taken the decision to try to win additional business revenue by effectively offering lower rates.
But he noted: "The move has been accepted by agents very well. I have spoken to several agents who find it a good move and are now waiting for other airlines."
United's Germany cargo sales manager, Robert Blythe, forecast Lufthansa Cargo might drop its surcharge on May 1 in response.
"I think Lufthansa will go on May 1 and after that it is a question of time when the others follow," he said.
Konrad Bossdorf, Air Canada cargo manager Germany, said he did not see a need to drop the fuel surcharge now since fuel prices had only gone down a few cents.
Swissair general cargo manager Germany, Ulf Steinmann, added: "If the national carrier (Lufthansa) stops, then we would look at the situation again. For us, the national carrier is decisive."
But a Lufthansa Cargo spokesman stressed it would first drop the surcharge when fuel prices returned to the levels of last July.
The lower deutschmark exchange rate against the U.S. dollar has clearly boosted airfreight exports to the Americas in recent weeks, industry observers said.
One German forwarder said: "There are strong export shipments at present because of the dollar development which is positive for the export industry."
Swissair's Steinmann said: "North America is going reasonably. A lot of over-capacity has been reduced and so rates are not so under pressure."
The high dollar was helping German air cargo exports but less than might be expected since companies were already awaiting a still stronger dollar, he said.
Delta manager Hass said the airline increased rates by 10 pfennigs per kg at the start of March in response to a strong market.
"Whoever does not increase rates at present has only himself to blame because he is missing out on extra revenue," he said.
"The market tendency is good. There is a lot of freight on the market and our flights are all full. We cannot give any more spot rates."
Atlanta was booming and exports had clearly risen because of the higher dollar exchange rate, Hass noted.
United's Blythe said the airline had also raised ex-Germany cargo rates by 10 percent and was seeing cargo load factors in the 90s.
"We are full two weeks in advance and I just hope it keeps going," he added.
Bossdorf, of Air Canada, said the airline would follow the rates trend with a 5-10 percent increase on April 1.
"The market seems to be very strong at present and the dollar is boosting exports," he said.
Demand for Latin America was generally good at present with heavy business to Mexico and Brazil and mixed signals for smaller destinations, sources said.
Swissair's Steinmann said: "South America has picked up well after the carnival season."
Iberia Germany sales manager, George von Doehren, said the Spanish carrier would hold ex-Germany cargo rates stable this spring since both demand and supply for Latin America were rising.
"We changed our rates in September and see no reason to change them at present. There will be no change," he said.
Von Doehren added: "January and February are always fairly slow because everyone is on holiday but demand is improving now and we have space problems."
The German air cargo market to Mexico is still growing strongly thanks to demand from the automotive industry generated by Volkswagen AG production plants, observers said.
Lufthansa Cargo sales manager Germany, Florian Pfaff, said: "There is extreme demand (for Mexico) due to Volkswagen. Demand is much higher than capacity."
Iberia's von Doehren said the airline currently had a waiting time of 4-5 days for smaller shipments on its daily Airbus A340 flights from Madrid to Mexico City and weekly DC-8 freighter service.
"Market demand is higher than we can offer to Mexico," he noted.
Load factors from Germany to Brazil were strong at present and good market growth was expected over the next few months, industry sources said.
In response, Varig would increase rates by four percent from April 1, they added.
Ishaq Shaikh, Germany cargo sales manager of Brazilian carrier VASP, said he had a high rates policy in line with Varig and Lufthansa since he could offer three weekly direct flights from Germany.
VASP was seeing good load factors, not only to Sao Paulo but also to Salvador and Recife, he said.
"January was a low month with Carnival and in February things picked up. If we now put all our efforts into sales, then I think we will have a backlog," he said.
Chilean carrier Lan Chile said it will add a fifth weekly B767-300 flight to Frankfurt via Sao Paulo and Madrid from April 8.
Cargo manager Europe, Martin Rehs, said the airline was currently considering whether to raise rates to selected Latin American destinations.
"Demand is good and better than this time last year. The opportunity to increase is certainly there. There are some destinations which need higher rates due to demand," he said.
Colombian airline Avianca said it has benefitted from the recent scrapping of Viasa and Lufthansa direct flights from Germany to Venezuela.
Viasa's three times a week DC-10 flights from Caracas to Frankfurt ended in early February while Lufthansa dropped its three weekly A340 flights at the start of March.
Dieter Uhl, managing director of Avianca GSA Air Impact Luftfahrtagentur, said: "We are very full and the market is going well. We now have more demand for Caracas as a fill up."
"At the moment, rates are stable. If market growth continues then there could be a rise," he added.
Colombia was a very stable market since companies had switched to European markets because of political difficulties with the USA, he pointed out.
Avianca flew Mondays and Fridays with a 767-300 from Frankfurt to Bogota with a Monday stopover in Caracas.
Von Doehren, of Iberia, which was Viasa GSA in Germany, said: "We had a lot of freight for Caracas and the aircraft had good load factors.
"We have certainly lost clients because they were companies who wanted to go directly to Caracas," he added.
Iberia also had regular freight to Colombia but most German shipments tended to go via Miami due to lower transhipment rates, he noted.
Cargo demand for southern Africa was steady at present but rates were still under pressure from tough competition, cargo sources said.
South African Airways said it will hold air cargo rates from Europe to South Africa stable this spring.
"SAA does not plan any rates increases from Europe to South Africa because the market does not support it," Wolfgang Els, its Europe cargo manager said.
"I hope that the rates level can be kept and that my competitors will start to think commercially," he added.
Air cargo exports to South Africa were likely to remain steady this year with no significant growth rates, he added.
"The market goes up and down in waves. What was not good for the market was the high capacity that came on to the market," he explained.

Ingo Zimmer, manager of ATC Aviation Services, GSA for Zimbabwe's freighter carrier Affretair, said: "I do not believe rates rises have been maintained. The big European carriers are breaking the rates."
Demand for Affretair's four weekly McDonnell Douglas DC-8 and DC-10 flights to Harare was growing well, with textiles, machines and chemicals as the main goods.
"Harare is going very well at present. There are a lot of chemicals being exported to Zimbabwe," he noted. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
